Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

📅 18 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand.
  • Recent findings suggest that that capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria.
  • In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a latest way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

Recent findings suggest that that capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

Light Powers and Steers the Tiny Robots.

In a recent development, one of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

Sources indicate that for the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an notable part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

It has been revealed that the latest control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

Nanorobots Act as "Microscopic Cleaners".

"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," indicates Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices.".

Industry observers note that the robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible.".

Industry observers note that the robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.
  • Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.
  • According to the BBC, the former Lapsus$ hacker has been released on license and given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including banning him from using Telegram and Discord.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.

Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.

According to the BBC, the former Lapsus$ hacker has been released on license and given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including banning him from using Telegram and Discord.

“You are a very talented young man,” Mr Justice Turner told Kurtaj before warning him: “Don’t let this happen again.”.

Kurtaj made headlines in September 2022 when he hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 clips containing nearly an hour of GTA 6 gameplay, revealing Vice City and the game’s two protagonists long before its official announcement.

Remarkably, the teenager carried out the attack while on bail for other cybercrimes, using an Amazon Fire Stick, a television, and a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse from a Travelodge hotel.

He also attempted to blackmail Rockstar, threatening to release the game’s source code unless the developer contacted him.

Rockstar later revealed that the breach cost the company approximately $5 million to recover from, alongside thousands of hours of staff time.

In December 2023, Kurtaj was sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital after being deemed unfit to stand trial due to his autism.

At the time, the court heard that he remained highly motivated to commit further cybercrimes and could potentially hack Rockstar again.

However, a subsequent assessment found him fit to stand trial, and he was moved to a conventional prison in January 2026.

Even while behind bars, Kurtaj made headlines again in March after allegedly using a smuggled phone to post about GTA 6. He later pleaded guilty to possessing a mobile phone in prison.

On November 16, Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the Rockstar hack and several other cybercrimes involving companies including Uber, Revolut, and BT/EE.

His release comes just days after GTA 6 officially released on November 19, more than four years after his original attack.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has faced another wave of GTA 6 leaks from the anonymous Cyberleek in 2026, including gameplay footage and claims of access to development builds.

#172397. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

📅 17 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1222 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

📅 17 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information.
  • Industry observers note that the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials.
  • The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

Industry observers note that the challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," noted Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely latest materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed.".

Building a Low Power Memory Device.

Using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

According to recent reports, that ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a newly introduced strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," noted Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Industry observers note that poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

"Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives.".

Engineering DNA to Conduct Electricity.

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

This technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

According to recent reports, synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

Industry observers note that "We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform.".

DNA and Perovskite Work Better Together.

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

According to recent reports, the carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

Industry observers note that the researchers also reported that the upcoming system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

Recent findings suggest that "Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane mentioned. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power.".

A Newly introduced Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics.

The team now plans to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

Sources indicate that "Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible.".

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

A cat has become an unlikely hero after helping stop a robbery in Mexico when its owner’s daughter picked it up and used the hissing feline to scare off an armed suspect.

The incident took place on November 7 at a family-owned grocery store in Puebla, Mexico, where a man threatened a woman working behind the counter.

However, the would-be thief hadn’t counted on the family’s cat, Misifú, who promptly turned the tables on him.

According to Mexico News Daily, the suspect initially entered the store in the San Ramón neighborhood and asked a woman named Lidia about medication.

He returned minutes later wearing a mask and hoodie, demanding money from the register while threatening to use a weapon allegedly concealed in his backpack.

That’s when Lidia’s daughter rushed to help, grabbing the family’s cat and holding it directly toward the robber’s face.

Rather than staying calm, Misifú began hissing and swiping at the suspect with its claws extended, scratching at his hands as he tried to protect himself.

The unusual defense worked, with the man backing away before eventually fleeing the store empty-handed.

Security camera footage of the incident went viral after being shared online on November 18, showing the suspect retreating as the cat repeatedly lashed out.

According to local outlet Tiempo, the family released the footage in hopes of identifying the would-be robber, who reportedly remains at large.

The family has also called for increased police patrols in the area following the attempted robbery.

It has been revealed that AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models quickly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

Sources indicate that AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Industry observers note that limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Recent findings suggest that vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

Industry observers note that hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page shows a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects swiftly.

Limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

Fits: creators who want images, video and avatars under one roof.

“Not stated” means the vendor page we reviewed did not say, not that the feature does not exist. Treat the table as a checklist of questions to answer in your own tests.

In a recent development, it depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Recent findings suggest that treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Recent findings suggest that start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Industry observers note that describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”.

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

According to recent reports, video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below highlights the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

It has been revealed that most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

It has been revealed that usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

Partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

Industry observers note that for short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

Sources indicate that it depends on the tool and initiative. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

Breaking: NASA just used satellites and debris to navigate without GPS

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.
  • The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence.
  • Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly important as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

It has been revealed that the FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

Sources indicate that "FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," noted Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing.".

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points.

The FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

Industry observers note that during position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

Recent findings suggest that A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation.

In a recent development, FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

These abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an crucial role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology.

According to recent reports, the FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

Recent findings suggest that later this year, Starling, which launched in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

TikTok star Ophelia Nichols, better known as Mama Tot, has spoken out after the man who fatally shot her teenage son was acquitted of murder.

Nichols, who has amassed over 12 million followers on TikTok, lost her 18-year-old son Randon Lee on June 24, 2022, after he was shot during an arranged drug deal outside a gas station in Prichard, Alabama, just one day before his 19th birthday.

Recent findings suggest that on November 20, 2026, a jury found 25-year-old Reuben Gulley not guilty of murder following roughly 90 minutes of deliberations. Gulley had admitted to shooting Lee but maintained that he acted in self-defense.

In a post on Facebook following the verdict, Nichols described watching her husband break down in tears inside the courtroom.

“I have watched my husband break down sitting in that courtroom today while I did my best to hold it together for myself, for him, my children, our entire family,” Nichols wrote.

“As I could feel the excited energy from the other side because their son was coming home, I slowly melted into my seat. Knowing that Justice had been stripped from my son and us, I couldn’t even describe what it did to my soul.”.

During the trial, Gulley testified that he had entered the back seat of Lee’s car to purchase two ounces of marijuana for $300. He claimed Lee pulled a gun on him after he took out the money, prompting him to open fire.

In a recent development, prosecutors argued that Gulley shot the teenager to avoid paying for the drugs. Surveillance footage showed him fleeing Lee’s vehicle with a gun in his hand, although it did not capture the shooting itself.

TikTok star Mama Tot “not happy” after man arrested in connection with son’s murder.

Man arrested in connection with murder of TikTok star Mama Tot’s son.

TikToker Ophelia Nichols appeals for information following son’s murder.

Gulley’s defense attorney, Chase Dearman, questioned the police investigation and argued there was insufficient evidence to convict his client.

Following the acquittal, Nichols remarked her family would continue to question how the jury reached its decision.

Industry observers note that “We don’t know what, why or how the jurors came to that decision and I’m sure we will question that moment the rest of our lives,” she wrote. “No remorse for our family. Zero regards for Randon’s life. What was done to our family was downright cruel and knowing that we are not alone in these situations is scary.”.

The TikToker also described the emotional toll the verdict had taken on her husband and daughter.

“I watched my daughter cry her eyes out today, I’ve only seen my husband cry like three times in the 20 years we’ve been married and he couldn’t control himself today,” she stated. “He lost it.”.

IBM quantum computer solves classically intractable problem in 15 minutes

📅 30 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists used a latest error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.
  • The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.
  • Industry observers note that IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists used a latest error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.

The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.

Industry observers note that IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage. The experiment performed a calculation beyond the practical reach of leading classical simulation techniques while also providing evidence that the quantum computer produced a reliable result.

In a latest paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers describe how they achieved both goals using a newly designed form of encoded quantum circuit. The work represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing reported so far.

The circuits and experimental results have also been made publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.

Why Quantum Results Are So Difficult to Verify.

Researchers have long used a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS) to explore whether quantum computers can outperform conventional machines.

Recent findings suggest that in simplified terms, RCS challenges a quantum computer to generate patterns that become so complicated that a classical computer cannot efficiently reproduce them. That makes the benchmark useful for testing the limits of classical simulation.

But it also creates a major problem. Once the quantum calculation becomes too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, verifying that the quantum machine actually produced the correct result becomes increasingly difficult as well. Eventually, checking the answer can itself become infeasible unless researchers make strong assumptions about how the quantum computer behaves internally.

The IBM and University of Chicago team approached this verification problem by developing a more structured alternative to RCS.

The researchers showed that their method preserves the same computational hardness criteria associated with RCS, meaning the problem remains extremely difficult for classical computers. At the same time, the added structure allows errors to be detected during the quantum computation.

It has been revealed that "Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem.".

Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers.".

70 Logical Qubits With Lower Error Rates.

The experiment also included one of the world's largest-known demonstrations of quantum error correction.

It has been revealed that the researchers operated 70 logical qubits. Unlike individual physical qubits, logical qubits are encoded in a way that helps protect quantum information from errors and noise.

Using those logical qubits, the team carried out 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates," two measures that reflect the complexity of the quantum circuit.

The encoded design significantly improved reliability. Effective logical error rates were 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates, allowing the circuit to maintain unusually high fidelity even while performing a large number of quantum operations.

IBM Claims Quantum Advantage Has Entered a Newly introduced Stage.

"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically.".

The researchers found that many leading classical simulation methods would face prohibitive runtimes when attempting the same task.

The IBM quantum computer, by comparison, completed the computation in approximately 15 minutes.

A Step Toward Larger, More Trustworthy Quantum Computers.

Speed alone is not enough for quantum computing to become useful at larger scales. Researchers also need ways to suppress errors and establish confidence that a quantum system produced a valid result.

This experiment advances both goals at once by combining large-scale logical quantum computing with a method for evaluating the reliability of a calculation that is already beyond practical classical simulation.

Error correction and trustworthy verification are considered essential for scaling quantum computers toward more difficult problems, making the upcoming demonstration an notable step toward that goal.

#172384. A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot

📅 31 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1022 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A “quantum bath” puts quantum entanglement on autopilot

📅 31 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, future quantum computers may depend on the ability to connect widely separated modules through distributed entanglement.
  • Recent findings suggest that published in Physical Review X, the experiment provides the first demonstration of a prediction proposed more than 20 years ago.
  • It has been revealed that entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, future quantum computers may depend on the ability to connect widely separated modules through distributed entanglement. Until now, creating this kind of connection has generally required active control and repeated measurements. Physicists at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) have now demonstrated a fully autonomous alternative based on a "quantum bath" made from correlated particles of light.

Recent findings suggest that published in Physical Review X, the experiment provides the first demonstration of a prediction proposed more than 20 years ago. The approach could eventually offer a newly introduced foundation for practical quantum technologies.

Connecting Distant Quantum Bits.

It has been revealed that entanglement is one of the defining phenomena of quantum physics. It allows particles or systems to share correlations that cannot be explained by classical physics. Creating distributed entanglement between physically separated qubits (quantum bits) could be notable for building larger quantum computers and future quantum networks.

Previous attempts to entangle distant qubits have generally followed one of two strategies. One method sends a single, actively controlled photon from one qubit to another. Another has each qubit emit a photon, with the two photons then matched in an effort to generate entanglement.

Sources indicate that the second approach was recognized by the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. However, it still depends on repeated measurements and post-selection, and even then, the process does not always successfully produce entanglement.

In a recent development, phD student Alejandro Andrés-Juanes and professor Johannes Fink at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) worked with international collaborators to develop a different solution. Their system uses a quantum bath that automatically brings distant qubits into synchronization. In a prototype device, the researchers used a shared source of correlated light particles to entangle two separated qubits, experimentally realizing an idea that had remained theoretical for more than two decades.

Fully Autonomous Quantum Entanglement.

According to recent reports, quantum entanglement can take several forms. Continuous-variable entangled states can be produced efficiently and are therefore relatively accessible. They can be compared with a pendulum, whose position and momentum change continuously.

Many useful quantum technologies, however, depend on "discrete-variable" systems. These involve 'all-or-nothing' forms of entanglement that stationary qubits can use. The challenge for the ISTA team was finding a way to connect these readily available continuous forms of entanglement with the discrete forms needed for practical applications.

Sources indicate that "In this work, we aimed to overcome this mismatch between the readily available and the practically useful forms of entanglement," says Andrés-Juanes. "By stabilizing the entangled states remotely, our approach is fully autonomous and requires no active control or measurement.".

A Quantum Bath Powered by Correlated Light.

Maintaining both entanglement and quantum coherence is one of the major difficulties facing quantum computing.

The researchers addressed that problem by making the qubits' surrounding environment itself responsible for producing and stabilizing entanglement.

According to recent reports, "In our method, the quantum bath -- meaning the qubits' environment -- is the source of entanglement. It creates a new ground state through a continuous stream of correlated photons," says Fink. "This way, the entangled qubit state is stabilized, even beyond the qubits' own 'lifetime', and remains always available as a resource for further quantum processing. This makes the approach conceptually significant.".

Because the entangled state remains available, researchers can access it whenever it is needed. That differs from temporary entanglement, which has to be used during the brief period when it exists.

Microwave Photons Keep Qubits Connected.

In a recent development, to couple the qubits with the entangled photon source, the researchers relied on microwave photons. These low-energy light particles are especially useful for manipulating quantum information and are already central to leading superconducting-qubit technology.

Industry observers note that optical photons serve a different role and are commonly used in optics and atomic physics. They may also become vital for carrying quantum information between distant quantum computers through fiber optics, an area that the Fink group at ISTA is also investigating.

Measuring the Hidden Quantum State.

The researchers needed to confirm that the two qubits were actually synchronized inside the quantum bath. To do that, they used quantum tomography, a technique that reconstructs a quantum system by examining many different 'slices' of its behavior.

"Qubits can be in a superposition of states, but all these states collapse when we measure them, leaving us with a 0 or 1 state," says Andrés-Juanes.

Sources indicate that quantum tomography allowed the researchers to perform measurements lasting only 20-80 nanoseconds and use those observations to investigate the qubits' underlying states. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second.

A 20-Year Prediction Becomes an Experiment.

By successfully entangling two isolated qubits through a quantum bath, the ISTA researchers created a proof-of-concept laboratory prototype for the long-standing theoretical proposal.

"We present a relatively simple method that could be scaled up to synchronize multiple distant qubits," says Andrés-Juanes.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced approach is promising, but it is not yet as efficient as methods that actively control qubit states. "Our method presently transfers about 10% of the bath's available entanglement.".

The researchers suggest that one reason the idea took more than two decades to demonstrate is that the original theory was developed under idealized conditions that are difficult to reproduce experimentally.

"Our experiments helped us reveal several factors that may have prevented scientists from designing a functional quantum bath using a single source of correlated photons for distributed entanglement," indicates Fink.

The prototype developed at ISTA could provide newly introduced opportunities for quantum-optics experiments. It may also contribute to efforts to expand quantum processors and ultimately move them closer to fault-tolerant operation.

A “Chinese spy” lookalike contest took over New York City’s Washington Square Park, with participants performing mock espionage acts for a cash prize.

The competition took place on November 21 and was organized by FactMachine and Prez, drawing a crowd of spectators who were given the opportunity to vote for their favorite contestants.

The event was inspired by the ongoing controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who had resigned as CEO just over a week before the competition took place.

Around 10 women participated in the competition, dressing up as spies and performing various espionage-inspired acts in front of the crowd.

In a recent development, the contest came after Nvidia introduced an independent investigation on November 8 into reports that its CEO had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang also admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a message sent to employees.

Industry observers note that on November 12, he resigned as president, CEO, and a member of Nvidia’s board of directors, ending his 33-year tenure leading the tech giant. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

However, just two days after the lookalike contest, Nvidia confirmed that Huang had been reinstated following a unanimous vote by its board of directors.

Recent findings suggest that the company said it had consulted senior US government officials and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. Its independent investigation remains ongoing, with Huang committing to cooperate.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

According to recent reports, this guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

The direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt notes Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: New accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

In a recent development, for developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free blueprint includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid aims start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

According to recent reports, pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid intends from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

In a recent development, murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

Pricing: Free strategy with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Sources indicate that speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

Industry observers note that the use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid intends are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

In a recent development, wellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

In a recent development, pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example demonstrates how little code a basic request takes:.

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

Recent findings suggest that the say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

Industry observers note that what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Recent findings suggest that is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free aims or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for newly introduced accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free initiative, which has no commercial licence.

Sources indicate that can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid looks, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

Recent findings suggest that what is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Sources indicate that which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

In a recent development, how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

Recent findings suggest that AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings.
  • According to recent reports, quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics.
  • A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

According to recent reports, quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Recent findings suggest that traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can rapidly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

According to recent reports, "The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information.

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

Sources indicate that "Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster.

Recent findings suggest that working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

In a recent development, chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," notes Lei Du.

Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

It has been revealed that these gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers.

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," notes Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an key role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control.

Sources indicate that *Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Sources indicate that quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

Recent findings suggest that the scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

  • Despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips for its ambitious data center projects and is using the semiconductors as collateral. However, Ars Technica reports that lenders are concerned that SpaceX will use the chips for its planned orbital data center, making it difficult, if not impossible, for creditors to reclaim in case the organization defaults on its loan. SpaceX stated it will deploy the collateralized chips only on Earth, but it remains unclear whether this provision is included in the signed debt instrument.

In a recent development, spaceX is working on building massive data centers on both Earth and in space. Musk has already revealed the firm’s first-generation AI1 satellite, with a 120-kilowatt payload and a span that’s larger than a Boeing 747, while he’s also planning to build a $24-billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas. These projects are in addition to the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 sites near the Tennessee-Mississippi border.

Despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected. Instead, it’s built similarly to aircraft leasing agreements, in which a leasing manufacturer buys the jets and leases them to the airline that wants to use them. This saves the airline from having to put up a significant amount of cash to get the airplanes that it needs.

For this deal, the Saturn Funding Trust, a fully owned subsidiary of asset-backed lending tech giant WHCO, would acquire the Nvidia GPUs for SpaceX, with the latter paying the former quarterly for the privilege of using the AI chips. The deal is also described as a “five-year triple-net, hell-or-high-water finance lease arrangement,” meaning SpaceX must pay the lease for five years, whether the chips break, become obsolete, or the project becomes unprofitable. It’s also responsible for all the expenses of operating the chips.

In a recent development, these terms are very lender-friendly, as SpaceX basically assumes all the risks while also keeping them off its books. Rating agency Moody’s also remarked in its report that the chips will be deployed in SpaceX’s U.S. data centers. Nevertheless, the manufacturer’s proposal to blast data centers into space is making some lenders nervous, regardless of its Earth-bound looks and promises.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discord’s new Auto Clips automatically saves gameplay moments when it hears a voice chat erupt in laughter or shouting, and it’s rolling out to Nitro members now.

Whether you’re playing a chaotic game of Fortnite or getting your friends together for another big Minecraft marathon, being able to instantly capture those moments that leave you in stitches of laughter is imperative.

After all, we’ve all been in situations where you’ve forgotten to hit record or your capture software has decided to stop working (it couldn’t be me). Enter Discord’s Auto Clips, a latest feature that can detect when your group starts laughing or shouting before pulling together a clip of what just happened.

According to recent reports, unlike other capture software, Discord Auto Clips removes the need to hit a keyboard shortcut to record clips. Instead, it uses a small machine learning model that runs locally on the user’s PC, which continuously looks for audio cues resembling laughter or shouting, then uses those reactions to flag moments that might be worth saving.

Discord has revealed that the model cannot understand conversations or identify individual speakers, while any footage that is not saved as a clip is discarded after the gaming session ends.

Auto Clips can also work without voice chat in Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, League of Legends, and Rocket League. Discord uses integrations with those games to recognize events such as kills, goals, and completed rounds, with support for more titles planned in the future.

Recent findings suggest that we've been cooking on Clips since Early Access introduced in 2023.Now there's 🢂Ａｕｔｏ Ｃｌｉｐｓ🢀When you and your friends break out laughing in voice, Discord saves the moment. No keybinds or additional setup needed. Starting today, Auto Clips is rolling out to Nitro… pic.twitter.com/a70itXDB1f.

According to recent reports, up to three highlights can be saved during each session, after which players can review them through Discord’s Clips library. It’s here that each recording can be trimmed, renamed, and edited with text or images, while game and voice audio can be removed before you share it with your friends or the wider internet.

Discord says clips remain stored locally on the player’s PC unless they choose to post them, and the company does not use saved footage, voice recordings, or other user data to train its detection model.

Sources indicate that if you want to opt out of the feature, Discord states that consumers will be able to disable Auto Clips entirely or prevent their voice from appearing in clips recorded by other people. The feature began rolling out to Nitro members in Early Access on November 24 and is right now only available through Discord’s Windows desktop app.
