But again, really nice work on this blog post and on Picotron guys!

Sources indicate that these are absolutely great pointer. Would you like to add your suggestions to the blog post directly? That way we could have you as one of the authors of the blog post (with due credits.).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, the project’s README says that the app allows reading of “GPU power, pin currents, and temperatures at a glance.” The per-pin monitoring is the notable part here, as the 12V-2x6 connection carries current on six 12V pins with a rating of about 9A, with Asus’s warning at 9.2A, and exceeding the per-pin limit has led to melted connectors.
  • According to recent reports, for supported Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs, the app uses the open-source LibreHardwareMonitor library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A developer known as Codeh4ck released a free, open-source Windows app, RTX Lens, to help assuage melting power connector fears for owners of powerful RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs. The app can read per-pin current information on Asus Astral cards, the WireView Pro II GPU monitoring device from Thermal Grizzly, and MSI MPG Ai1300TS/Ai1600TS PSUs, enabling an optional shutdown for persistent warnings. It works by reading current at the GPU, PSU, or both ends of the cable, and can even notify you by phone to provide extra protection for your investment.

According to recent reports, the project’s README says that the app allows reading of “GPU power, pin currents, and temperatures at a glance.” The per-pin monitoring is the notable part here, as the 12V-2x6 connection carries current on six 12V pins with a rating of about 9A, with Asus’s warning at 9.2A, and exceeding the per-pin limit has led to melted connectors. An RTX 5090 is rated at 575W of board power, which is close to the connector’s 600W rating. This led to the app’s construction, the developer says, due to “double paranoia about the 12VHPWR connector melting, since I own 2 5090s.”.

According to recent reports, for supported Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs, the app uses the open-source LibreHardwareMonitor library. The WireView Pro II already measures inline at the GPU connector, but the app can read and edit the device’s settings, mirroring the official app’s settings.

In a recent development, the MSI PSUs measure at the PSU side of each connector and reveal per-pin currents for both 12V-2x6 ports, as well as PSU temperature and fan status, although a USB data connection is needed for both the PSUs and the WireView. The project clarifies that “With an Astral or WireView Pro II, you can compare both ends of the cable.” All of the listed hardware has been tested on real devices, the developer indicates.

Connector power, current totals.

Thermal Grizzly WireView Pro II.

Clocks, temps, usage, VRAM, fans.

The app allows customers to set up warning profiles per device with thresholds and reminders, and optionally a shutdown when a warning persists. This would be used in cases of sustained overcurrent or uneven pin loads on Astral, or WireView device faults. The app’s service initiates a Windows shutdown after a set time, from one second to almost 24 hours. The app can also make performance recordings that are exportable as interactive HTML.

In a recent development, additionally, it can configure MSI Afterburner Safeguard+ for the MSI PSUs with per-connector alarms and timeouts, emergency low-power profiles, or even a script for delayed shutdowns or optional methods of notification, like email. More customization is available, in this case, as the app can set the PSUs’ fan curves with up to six temperature points.

It has been revealed that phone apps for Android, using a sideloaded APK from GitHub, and the iPhone, through a TestFlight beta or sideloaded with iLoader, are available. The sideloaded iPhone app only shows warnings while it’s open and connected, though. Pairing happens by QR code on the same network, and remote access from outside the network requires a reachable address. The PC also must stay awake, with the service running, for local or remote connections to work. An alternative way to monitor is a read-only iCUE widget for the Corsair Xeneon Edge touchscreen, if you’re so inclined.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

It has been revealed that the ongoing melting connector problem has led to solutions in the past, including a vibe-coded safeguard that now limits the GPU if a pin current exceeds 9.5A for more than 15 seconds, then shuts down the system if it stays that high. That tool, 12VHPWR Guard, is limited to Asus cards; RTX Lens adds wider device support and more options. Some hardware already works to help here, as MSI’s Ai1600TS cut GPU power after about three minutes in our testing, and Cooler Master’s GPU Shield can scale down an RTX 5090 to 450W, but these are not an option, or the best option, for everyone.

Sources indicate that RTX Lens updates have been fast, with five shipped releases in the last week or so, and the maintainer appears motivated to keep development going. The developer says the project is in a “beta-ish phase,” and that “Google Play Store and App Store releases are coming soon, pending approval from Google and Apple.”.

Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

💡 Key Takeaways

In a recent development, power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

The agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

According to recent reports, we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

In a recent development, the second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

Which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a newly introduced measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

In a recent development, names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

It has been revealed that the formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

Sources indicate that relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

According to recent reports, to see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

Sources indicate that on 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

Sources indicate that the measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

It returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Sources indicate that think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

In a recent development, this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

One detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

Good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

Naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a latest colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

In a recent development, microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

An agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Sources indicate that start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and noted it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

Recent findings suggest that the --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

According to recent reports, version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

Industry observers note that an agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer newly introduced to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

It has been revealed that these are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

Take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

Three Mighty Alerts Supporting Hugging Face’s Production Infrastructure

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Infrastructure team at Hugging Face is excited to share a behind-the-scenes look at the inner workings of Hugging Face's production infrastructure, which we’ve had the privilege of helping to build and maintain. Our team's dedication to designing and implementing a robust monitoring and alerting system has been instrumental in ensuring the stability and scalability of our platforms. We’re constantly reminded of the impact that our alerts have on our ability to identify and respond to potential issues before they become major incidents.

In this blog post, we’ll dive into the details of three mighty alerts that play their unique role in supporting our production infrastructure, and explore how they've helped us maintain the high level of performance and uptime that our community relies on.

Oftentimes, with cloud computing architectures, where data flows between private and public networks, implementing a NAT (Network Address Translation) gateway stands as a steadfast best practice. This gateway acts as a strategic gatekeeper, monitoring and facilitating all outbound traffic towards the public Internet. By centralizing egress traffic, the NAT gateway offers a strategic vantage point for comprehensive visibility. Our team can easily query and analyze this traffic, making it an invaluable asset when working through security, cost optimization or various other investigative scenarios.

Industry observers note that cost optimization is a critical aspect of cloud infrastructure management, and understanding the pricing dynamics is key. In data centers, pricing structures often differentiate between east-west traffic (typically communication within the same rack or building) and north-south traffic (communication between further away private networks or the internet). By monitoring network traffic volume, Hugging Face gains valuable insights into these traffic patterns. This awareness allows us to make informed decisions regarding infrastructure configuration and architecture, ensuring we limit incurring needless costs.

Recent findings suggest that one of our key alerts is designed to notify us when our network traffic volume surpasses a predefined threshold. This alert serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it acts as an early warning system, alerting us to any unusual spikes in traffic that might indicate potential issues or unexpected behavior. Secondly, it prompts us to regularly review our traffic trends, ensuring we stay on top of our infrastructure's growth and evolving needs. This alert is set at a static threshold, which we have fine-tuned over time, ensuring it remains relevant and effective. When triggered, it often coincides with periods of refactoring our infrastructure.

For instance, when integrating third-party security and autoscaling tools, we've observed increased telemetry data egress from our nodes, triggering the alert and prompting us to optimize our configurations.

On another occasion, adjustments to our infrastructure lead to mistakenly avoiding a private, low-cost path between product-specific infrastructure (ex. traffic destined to the Hub from a Space to interact with repository data). To elaborate further, the most impactful workloads in terms of cost savings we’ve found are those that access object storage. Fetching objects directly prices cheaper than going through CDN-hosted assets for our LFS repository storage and additionally does not require the same security measures that our WAF provides compared to public requests arriving at our front door. Leveraging DNS overrides to switch traffic through private network paths and public network paths has become a valuable technique for us, driven by the CDKTF AWS provider.

As a final note, while we have configuration-as-code ensuring the desired state is always in effect, having an additional layer of alerting around helps in case mistakes are made when expressing the desired state through code.

The logging infrastructure at Hugging Face is a sophisticated system designed to collect, process, and store vast amounts of log data generated by our applications and services. At the heart of this system is the Hub application logging pipeline, a well-architected solution that ensures Hub model usage data is efficiently captured, enriched, and stored for reporting and archival purposes. The pipeline begins with Filebeat, a lightweight log shipper that runs as a daemonset alongside our application pods in each Kubernetes cluster. Filebeat's role is to collect logs from various sources, including application containers, and forward them to the next stage of the pipeline.

According to recent reports, once logs are collected by Filebeat, they are sent to Logstash, a powerful log processing tool. Logstash acts as the data processing workhorse, applying a series of mutations and transformations to the incoming logs. This includes enriching logs with GeoIP data for geolocation insights, routing logs to specific Elasticsearch indexes based on predefined criteria, and manipulating log fields by adding, removing, or reformatting them to ensure consistency and ease of analysis. After Logstash has processed the logs, they are forwarded to an Elasticsearch cluster.

Elasticsearch, a distributed search and analytics engine, forms the core of our log storage and analysis platform. It receives the logs from Logstash and applies its own set of processing rules through Elasticsearch pipelines. These pipelines perform minimal processing tasks, such as adding timestamp fields to indicate the time of processing, which is crucial for log analysis and correlation. Elasticsearch provides a scalable and flexible storage solution, allowing us to buffer logs for operational use and real-time analysis.

To manage the lifecycle of logs within Elasticsearch, we employ a robust storage and lifecycle management strategy. This ensures that logs are retained in Elasticsearch for a defined period, providing quick access for operational and troubleshooting purposes. After this retention period, logs are offloaded to long-term archival storage. The archival process involves an automated tool that reads logs from Elasticsearch indexes, formats them as Parquet files—an efficient columnar storage format—and writes them to our object storage system.

The final stage of our logging pipeline leverages AWS data warehousing services. Here, AWS Glue crawlers are utilized to discover and classify data in our object storage, automatically generating a Glue Data Catalog, which provides a unified metadata repository. The Glue table schema is periodically refreshed to ensure it remains up-to-date with the evolving structure of our log data. This integration with AWS Glue enables us to query the archived logs using Amazon Athena, a serverless interactive query service. Athena allows us to run SQL queries directly against the data in object storage, providing a cost-effective and scalable solution for log analysis and historical data exploration.

In a recent development, another point of fragility is the auto-schema detection mechanism in Elasticsearch. While it is designed to adapt to changing log structures, it can fail when application logs undergo significant field type changes. If the schema detection fails to recognize the new field types, it may lead to failed writes from Logstash to Elasticsearch, causing log processing bottlenecks and potential data inconsistencies. This matter highlights the importance of proactive log schema management and the need for robust monitoring to detect and address such issues promptly.

According to recent reports, memory management is also a critical aspect of the pipeline's stability. The log processing tier, including Logstash and Filebeat, operates with limited memory resources to control costs. When backpressure occurs, these components can experience Out-of-Memory (OOM) complications, especially during system slowdowns. As logs accumulate and backpressure increases, the memory footprint of these processes grows, pushing them closer to their limits. If not addressed promptly, this can lead to process crashes or further exacerbation of the backpressure problem.

Archival jobs, responsible for transferring logs from Elasticsearch to object storage, have also encountered challenges. On occasion, these jobs can be resource-intensive, with their performance becoming sensitive to node size and memory availability. In cases where junk data or unusually large log entries pass through the pipeline, they can strain the archival process, leading to failures due to memory exhaustion or node capacity limits. This underscores the importance of data validation and filtering earlier in the pipeline to prevent such problems from reaching the archival stage.

According to recent reports, to mitigate these potential failures, we've implemented a powerful alert system with a unique motivation: validating end-to-end log flow. The alert is designed to compare the number of requests received by our Application Load Balancer (ALB) with the number of logs successfully archived, providing a comprehensive view of log data flow throughout the entire pipeline. This approach allows us to promptly identify any discrepancies that might indicate potential log loss or processing challenges.

In a recent development, the alert mechanism is based on a simple yet effective comparison: the number of requests hitting our ALB, which represents the total log volume entering the system, versus the number of logs successfully archived in our long-term storage. By monitoring this ratio, we can ensure that what goes in must come out, providing a robust validation of our logging infrastructure's health. When the alert is triggered, it indicates a potential mismatch, prompting immediate investigation and remediation.

Industry observers note that in practice, this alert has proven to be a valuable tool, especially during periods of infrastructure refactoring. For instance, when we migrated our ALB to a VPC origin, the alert was instrumental in identifying and addressing the resulting log flow discrepancies. However, it has also saved us in less obvious scenarios. For example, when archive jobs failed to run due to unforeseen problems, the alert flagged the missing archived logs, allowing us to promptly investigate and resolve the problem before it impacted our log analysis and retention processes.

It has been revealed that while this alert is a powerful tool, it is just one part of our comprehensive monitoring strategy. We continuously refine and adapt our logging infrastructure to handle the ever-increasing volume and complexity of log data. By combining proactive monitoring, efficient resource management, and a deep understanding of our system's behavior, Hugging Face ensures that our logging pipeline remains resilient, reliable, and capable of supporting our platform's growth and evolving needs. This alert is a testament to our commitment to maintaining a robust and transparent logging system, providing our teams with the insights they need to keep Hugging Face running smoothly.

It has been revealed that when operating cloud-native applications and Kubernetes-based infrastructures, even seemingly minor issues can escalate into significant downtime if left unchecked. This is particularly true for the Kubernetes API, which serves as the central nervous system of a Kubernetes cluster, orchestrating the creation, management, and networking of containers. At Hugging Face, we've learned through experience that monitoring the Kubernetes API error rate and rate limiting metrics is a crucial practice, one that can prevent potential disasters.

In a recent development, hugging Face's infrastructure is deeply integrated with Kubernetes, and the kube-rs library has been instrumental in building and managing this ecosystem efficiently. kube-rs offers a Rust-centric approach to Kubernetes application development, providing developers with a familiar and powerful toolkit. At its core, kube-rs introduces three key concepts: reflectors, controllers, and custom resource interfaces. Reflectors ensure real-time synchronization of Kubernetes resources, enabling applications to react swiftly to changes. Controllers, the decision-makers, continuously reconcile the desired and actual states of resources, making Kubernetes self-healing. Custom resource interfaces extend Kubernetes, allowing developers to define application-specific resources for better abstraction.

Additionally, kube-rs introduces watchers and finalizers. Watchers monitor specific resources for changes, triggering actions in response to events. Finalizers, on the other hand, ensure proper cleanup and resource termination by defining custom logic. By providing Rust-based abstractions for these Kubernetes concepts, kube-rs allows developers to build robust, efficient applications, leveraging the Kubernetes platform's power and flexibility while maintaining a Rust-centric development approach. This integration streamlines the process of building and managing complex Kubernetes applications, making it a valuable tool in Hugging Face's infrastructure.

Sources indicate that hugging Face's integration with Kubernetes is a cornerstone of our infrastructure, and the kube-rs library plays a pivotal role in managing this ecosystem. The kube::api:: module is instrumental in automating various tasks, such as managing HTTPS certificates for custom domains supporting our Spaces product. By programmatically handling certificate lifecycles, we ensure the security and accessibility of our services, providing owners with a seamless experience. Additionally, we have used this module outside of user-facing features during routine maintenance to facilitate node draining and termination providing cluster stability during infrastructure updates.

Industry observers note that the kube::runtime:: module has been equally crucial for us, enabling the development and deployment of custom controllers that enhance our infrastructure's automation and resilience. For instance, we've implemented controllers for billing management in our managed services, where watchers and finalizers on customer pods ensure accurate resource tracking and billing. This level of customization allows us to adapt Kubernetes to our specific needs.

Through kube-rs, Hugging Face has achieved a high level of efficiency, reliability, and control over our cloud-native applications. The library's Rust-centric design aligns with our engineering philosophy, allowing us to leverage Rust's strengths in managing Kubernetes resources. By automating critical tasks and building custom controllers, we've created a scalable, self-healing infrastructure that meets the diverse and evolving needs of our owners and enterprise customers. This integration demonstrates our commitment to harnessing the full potential of Kubernetes while maintaining a development approach tailored to our unique requirements.

While our infrastructure rarely encounters issues related to the Kubernetes API, we remain vigilant, especially during and after deployments. The Kubernetes API is a critical component in our use of kube::runtime:: for managing customer pods and cloud networking resources. Any disruptions or inefficiencies in API communication can have cascading effects on our services, potentially leading to downtime or degraded performance.

In a recent development, the importance of monitoring these API metrics is underscored by the experiences of other users of Kubernetes. OpenAI, for instance, shared a status enhancement detailing how DNS availability issues resulted in significant downtime. While not directly related to the Kubernetes API, their experience highlights the interconnectedness of various infrastructure components and the potential for cascading failures. Just as DNS availability is vital for application accessibility, a healthy and responsive Kubernetes API is essential for managing and orchestrating our containerized workloads.

As a best practice, we've integrated these API metrics into our monitoring and alerting systems, ensuring that any anomalies or trends are promptly brought to our attention. This allows us to take a proactive approach, investigating and addressing issues before they impact our customers. For instance, on one occasion a single cluster started rate limiting requests to the Kubernetes API. We were able to trace this back to one of our third-party tools hitting a bug and repeatedly requesting a node be drained even though it had already done so. In response we were able to flush the malfunctioning job from the system before any noticeable degradation impacted our consumers. This is a great example that alerting scenarios do not just happen directly after deploying latest versions of our custom controllers — bugs can take time to manifest as production issues.

In conclusion, while our infrastructure is robust and well-architected, we recognize that vigilance and proactive monitoring are essential to maintaining its health and stability. By keeping a close eye on the Kubernetes API error rate and rate limiting metrics, we safeguard our managed services, ensure smooth customer experiences, and uphold our commitment to reliability and performance. This is a testament to our belief that in the world of cloud-native technologies, every component, no matter how small, plays a significant role in the overall resilience and success of our platform.

And a final bonus alert for reading through this far into the post!

At Hugging Face, our experiments are constantly in flux, often with purpose-fit clusters spinning up and down as we iterate on features and products. To add to the entropy, our growth is also a significant factor, with clusters expanding to their limits and triggering meiosis-like splits to maintain balance. To navigate this dynamic environment without resorting to hardcoding or introducing an additional cluster discovery layer, we've devised a clever alert that adapts to these changes.

According to recent reports, the metric used in this query is container_network_transmit_packets_total, which represents the total number of packets transmitted by a container. The query is filtering for metrics from a cluster’s local Prometheus instance, which is tasked with metric collection as well as remote writing to our central metric store — Grafana Mimir. Transmission of packets approximates healthy remote writes, which is what we want to ensure across all active clusters.

The first part of the query performs a current rate check. The second part of the query performs a historical rate check by using the same calculation as the current rate check plus an offset 48h clause. The -1 * multiplication is used to invert the result, so that if the historical rate is greater than 0, the result will be less than 0.

The or operator combines the two parts of the query. The query will return true if either of the following conditions is met:.

The outer < 0 condition checks if the result of the or operation is less than 0. This means that the query will only trigger if neither of the conditions is met, i.e., if a cluster has never sent any metrics (both current and historical rates are 0).

There are two cases where the query will trigger:.

In both cases, the query will detect that the cluster is not sending any metrics and trigger the alert.

It has been revealed that this simple yet effective solution fires in scenarios where our metrics infrastructure crashes, during cluster setup, and when they're torn down providing us with timely insights into our infrastructure's health. While it may not be the most critical alert in our arsenal, it holds a special place since it was born out of collaboration. It is a testament to the power of teamwork through rigorous code review, made possible by the expertise and willingness to help of fellow colleagues in the Hugging Face infrastructure team 🤗.

  • Perhaps worryingly, the United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) published its own report in which it warned that "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon." Such a move would be a violation of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Western intelligence agencies believe that Russia could be readying the launch of a nuclear-armed satellite before the end of the year. The satellite, called Sputnik-S, is believed to have been in development for the last several years, with the United States first warning of Russia's plans in February 2023. Now, a German news report believes that the country's armed forces are already "raising the alarm" about the potential impact such a satellite could have. According to one expert, such a weapon could knock out a third of low Earth orbit satellites instantly, eventually disabling all of them with a devastating impact on the planet as a whole. With satellites playing such a vital role for civilian life as well as both military and intelligence operations, it's easy to see why Russia may want such satellite-crippling capabilities.

The report notes that information about Sputnik-S has been exchanged between several NATO member countries, with intelligence agencies having already warned that a launch could happen within 60 days. That report was made in early November, suggesting that Sputnik-S could be in orbit and operational in early December. The Russian embassy in Germany rejected the "unfounded allegations," saying that they are nothing more than "part of a propaganda campaign" against the country.

Perhaps worryingly, the United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) published its own report in which it warned that "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon." Such a move would be a violation of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. The treaty prohibits any country from launching anything carrying nuclear weapons or, indeed, any weapon of mass destruction into Earth orbit. While there has been no suggestion that Russia could turn the nuclear weapons towards the planet, Sputnik-S would still clearly be in breach of the longstanding treaty. One expert cited by the report claims that a nuclear explosion in space would knock out one-third of low Earth orbit satellites instantly, with the remaining satellites gradually failing in the following months. The EMP generated could even cause widespread technical carnage on Earth.

In a recent development, as for which satellites could be a potential target for Sputnik-S, there is no shortage of options. SpaceX Starlink satellites are relied upon around the globe for their ability to provide fast, reliable networking to parts of the world not served by traditional connectivity options. Notably, Starlink has been used by Ukraine as it defends itself amid Russian aggression. But amid SpaceX's limiting of performance, Ukrainian officials have chosen to use their own "flying modems" to avoid relying on Elon Musk's company. Russia has been trying to launch its own Starlink rival, with limited success. September saw it lose a batch of 16 satellites during launch.

#172275. Industry News: Your AI Agent Inventory Is Already Wrong

Industry News: Your AI Agent Inventory Is Already Wrong

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Forbes

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Davie Sweis is Chief Data and AI Officer, Bosch Mobility, at Bosch.
  • Sooner or later, someone will ask you for a complete list of the AI systems operating on your firm’s data, with a named owner for each one.
  • Industry observers note that most companies can’t produce that list today, and I don’t think it’s carelessness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Davie Sweis is Chief Data and AI Officer, Bosch Mobility, at Bosch.

Sooner or later, someone will ask you for a complete list of the AI systems operating on your firm’s data, with a named owner for each one. It could be a regulator, an auditor or your security team during an incident. “We’re pulling that together” won’t be an acceptable answer.

Industry observers note that most companies can’t produce that list today, and I don’t think it’s carelessness. The reason is the way the list gets built.

It has been revealed that start with what we’re counting. An AI agent is software that takes a goal, plans its own steps and acts on them without a person approving each one. It files, routes, books and escalates. The inventory also has to cover AI features inside software you already license, which can arrive in a routine revision and be making decisions before anyone has reviewed them.

In a recent development, these systems enter the manufacturer in three ways: Your own teams build them, they get switched on inside platforms you already license, and employees adopt tools on their own. Netskope’s 2026 Cloud and Threat Report, drawn from its customers’ network traffic, found that 47% of people using generative AI at work still do so through personal accounts. Those accounts sit outside purchasing records, and a spreadsheet won’t keep up with them.

The EU AI Act keeps its oversight, monitoring and incident-reporting duties for organizations that deploy high-risk systems, even though this year’s amendment pushed the deadlines out to late 2027 and 2028. The later dates don’t change the first step: knowing which of your systems are covered.

Security puts the same pressure on a shorter clock. In October 2026, Axios reported that third-party AI agents had been accessing customer accounts at several large U.S. banks, some acting without the customer’s instruction. Every incident asks the question those banks faced: Which agent acted, under whose authority and on what? In a business-to-business setting, where partners’ agents will increasingly act inside your systems, you can only answer it if registering an agent is part of letting it in.

So, why doesn’t the list exist? The natural place to look is the platform console, which every major vendor now ships. Each sees its own environment, and beyond it, only as far as its connectors reach. There are also products that pull records from several platforms into one view. Whether you buy one or build your own, responsibility for what the list covers, which sources are connected and what happens when a record is missing stays with you.

Sources indicate that in the early 2000s, Universal Description, Discovery and Integration, or UDDI, promised a universal directory of web services, backed by IBM, Microsoft and SAP. The public registry closed in 2006. Web services could run without being published to it, so keeping the directory current was never a condition of deploying anything.

Kubernetes, the open-source system behind much of today’s cloud software, offers the opposite design. Once a team defines a Service—the stable address Kubernetes gives an application—the cluster publishes that name for other applications to find. There’s no separate registration step to forget.

For a large enterprise, that’s the design I would copy: Make inventory updates part of how you deploy and buy software, not a separate reporting task someone has to remember.

In practice, three feeds keep one list current:.

It has been revealed that 1. Systems You Build: Put the owner and a short description in the file used to deploy the agent, and have the release process publish the record whenever the agent is created, changed or retired. Nobody fills out a separate form.

2. Software You Rent: Use the vendor’s interface or a scheduled export to collect records, backed by a contract clause requiring updates when the AI features change.

It has been revealed that 3. Everything Nobody Declared: Use your network and sign-in logs to flag AI activity that was never registered, and route the findings to someone for review. The strongest version of this feed is a gateway: If every agent’s calls to AI models pass through one point you control, that point sees every call, and if each call carries the agent’s identity, it sees every agent, declared or not.

The same feeds have to carry changes and retirements, not only fresh entries, and someone has to own the records that come back incomplete.

Sources indicate that vendors have started building parts of this. In June 2026, Google, Microsoft and other partners announced Agentic Resource Discovery, a draft specification for publishing AI capability descriptions that compatible registries can read. In August 2026, AWS made its Agent Registry generally available, with an option to detect agents on its own agent platform. The first covers publishing across organizations and the second, detection inside one platform. You still decide which sources to connect and who reviews the gaps.

According to recent reports, the next practical step is to ask procurement and legal to add an inventory clause to upcoming software renewals, not only the ones labeled AI: The vendor provides a machine-readable list of the AI features and agents used on your data, with stable identifiers, and updates it when features are activated, changed or retired. Then have the responsible team test whether that export can create, patch and retire records in your inventory.

Recent findings suggest that the next time someone asks what AI is operating on your data, you want an answer that was true before they asked. Start with the next deployment and the next renewal, and make sure each one leaves a record your team can keep using.

Industry News: SmolLM3: smol, multilingual, long-context reasoner

📅 08 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Small language models are becoming increasingly important as people seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently.
  • SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot.
  • The complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Small language models are becoming increasingly important as people seek capable models that can be deployed efficiently. The community has produced a fascinating range of capable small models, each pushing the boundaries of what's possible at this scale. With SmolLM3, we're excited to contribute a new competitive fully open 3B model:.

SmolLM3 sits in the efficiency sweet spot. Our 3B model outperforms Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B while staying competitive with larger 4B alternatives (Qwen3 & Gemma3). Beyond the performance numbers, we're sharing exactly how we built it using public datasets and training frameworks.

The complete recipe: We're releasing SmolLM3 with our engineering blueprint. It includes architecture details, exact data mixtures showing how we progressively boost performance across domains in a three-stage pretraining approach, and the methodology for building a hybrid reasoning model. Usually, achieving these results would require months of reverse engineering. Instead, we're providing the full methodology.

Whether you're building your own models or want to understand what drives performance at this scale, this blueprint shows the engineering story behind competitive 3B performance.

Let’s have a look at the pretraining stage.

Industry observers note that smolLM3 both changed the architecture and data mixture over its predecessors. Let’s have a look at the architecture and training configurations first!

SmolLM3 follows a transformer decoder architecture with tied embedding similar to SmolLM2, building on Llama architecture with some key modifications optimized for efficiency and long context performance.

Grouped Query Attention (GQA): We replaced multi-head attention with grouped-query attention using 4 groups. Our ablations on a 3B model trained with 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu indicated that GQA matches the performance of multi-head attention while significantly reducing the KV cache size during inference.

NoPE: We implemented NoPE from "RoPE to NoRoPE and Back Again: A Newly introduced Hybrid Attention Strategy" (Yang et al., 2025), selectively removing rotary position embeddings from every 4th layer. This approach improves long context performance without affecting short context capabilities, as confirmed by our ablations.

Intra-Document Masking: Following "Analysing The Impact of Sequence Composition on Language Model Pre-Training", during training, we use attention masking to ensure tokens from different documents in the same training sequence don't attend to each other. Similar to Llama 3, this helps with faster and more stable long context training while maintaining short context performance.

Recent findings suggest that training Stability: Following OLMo 2, we remove weight decay from embedding layers to improve training stability. This modification contributed to more stable training dynamics, with embedding norms naturally stabilizing at healthier values during training without impacting overall performance in our ablations.

All these changes were validated through ablations using the same 3B architecture trained on 100B tokens from FineWeb-Edu, ensuring each modification either improved performance or maintained it while offering other benefits.

Training Configuration: We use a global batch size of 2.36M tokens with 4096 sequence length, a learning rate of 2e-4, and the AdamW optimizer (beta1: 0.9, beta2: 0.95) with weight decay of 0.1 and gradient clipping of 1. We use the WSD (Warmup-Stable-Decay) scheduler, with 2000  warmup steps, and a linear decay to 0 in the final 10% training steps. We use nanotron framework for the training, datatrove for data processing and lighteval for evaluation. The model was trained on 384 H100 GPUs for 24 days. You can see the distributed training setup in the following figure.

In addition to architecture changes we also ablated and improved the training recipe. Let’s have a closer look.

In a recent development, following SmolLM2's multi-stage approach, we train SmolLM3 on 11.2T tokens using a three-stage training strategy that mixes web, math, and code data with evolving proportions. We conducted extensive ablations on 3B models trained on 50B to 100B tokens to determine the data mixture and ratios.

The pretraining consists of these stages, also shown in the figure above:.

With these stages and mixtures we achieved very competitive performance for the base model. More on that in the evaluation section. The nanotron training configs with exact data weights can be found here. We will also share our training logs along with intermediate checkpoints.

After the main pretraining we improved the model in a mid-training stage for long context and reasoning.

We call the long context adaptation and reasoning adaptation “mid-training”. They are much shorter than the main pretraining but still somewhat general and aimed at improving the model in those two domains. Let’s first have a look at long context training.

After the main pretraining, we trained SmolLM3 on an additional 100B tokens to extend its context length. We sequentially extended the context window in two stages for 50B tokens each: first transitioning from 4k to 32k context with RoPE theta increased to 1.5M, then from 32k to 64k context with RoPE theta increased to 5M. Both stages upsampled math, code, and reasoning data. During ablations, we found that upsampling specific long context data such as code repositories, books, and long web pages (beyond the naturally long samples in our mixture) didn't further boost performance on RULER and HELMET benchmarks. Using NoPE and training on the decay mixture with longer sequences and increased RoPE theta values was sufficient to achieve competitive long context performance up to 64k.

Following Qwen2.5, we use YARN to extrapolate beyond the training context length. During inference, the model can handle up to  128k context (2x extension beyond the 64k training length).

After extending the context length of the model, we trained it at a mid-training stage to incorporate reasoning capabilities. The main difference between the mid-training stage and the pre- and post-training stages is that we targeted a general capability without yet focusing on a specific domain. In our case, we wanted to train the model to reason without targeting a particular domain, such as mathematics or computer code.

Our mid-training dataset contained 35B tokens sourced from Open Thought’s OpenThoughts3-1.2M and a subset from NVIDIA’s Llama-Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v1.1 with reasoning traces from R1. We used the ChatML chat template and wrapped packing to avoid providing too much structure to the model. We trained the model for 4 (~140B tokens) epochs and used the checkpoint for subsequent SFT stages.

The release of reasoning models like DeepSeek R1 and Qwen3 has demonstrated the powerful capabilities that emerge when models can engage in explicit reasoning. However, the community still lacks fully open recipes with public datasets to build dual instruction models that support both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Most existing approaches involve complex reinforcement learning processes and proprietary datasets, making it difficult for researchers to reproduce and build upon these results.

Industry observers note that in this section, we explain how we tackled these challenges and share our complete recipe for building a dual instruction model. We detail how we balance performance between reasoning and non-reasoning modes through a carefully designed training pipeline that includes mid-training for general reasoning capabilities, supervised fine-tuning with synthetic data generation, and alignment using Anchored Preference Optimization (APO) - a recent variant of DPO.

Before diving into the training methodology, it's essential to establish how users interact with our dual-mode model. The chat template serves as the interface that enables seamless switching between reasoning and non-reasoning modes, and its design directly impacts both our training data format and model behavior. SmolLM3's chat template allows users to control the reasoning mode during a conversation. Users can activate reasoning or non-reasoning modes by including the /think and /no_think flags, respectively, in the system prompt. In non-reasoning mode, we pre-fill the model's response with empty think blocks, similar to Qwen3, to ensure direct answers without explicit reasoning.

SmolLM3 supports tool calling, and its chat template incorporates two distinct sections for tool descriptions: XML Tools and Python Tools. This specific categorization proved beneficial in our experiments for the model's accurate interpretation of tool definitions in each format.

The chat template provides a default system message for both reasoning modes, along with a metadata section that includes the date, knowledge cut-off date, and current reasoning mode. Users can replace the default system message by providing one with the system role. The metadata section can be excluded by using the /system_override flag in the system prompt, offering flexibility for specific use cases.

Sources indicate that following the reasoning mid-training stage, where we trained the model on 140B tokens of general reasoning data, we proceed with Supervised Finetuning (SFT) to incorporate capabilities across both reasoning and non-reasoning modes for math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, multilinguality, and tool calling. Training a dual-mode model requires carefully balancing the data mixture to maintain strong performance in both modes across all target domains. To evaluate SmolLM3’s performance throughout training, we tracked the following domains: math, code, general reasoning, instruction following, and multilinguality.

Sources indicate that the primary challenge we encountered when building the reasoning mode dataset was the scarcity of datasets containing reasoning traces for certain domains. To address this gap, we generated synthetic data by prompting Qwen3-32B in reasoning mode with prompts from existing non-reasoning datasets. This allowed us to improve performance in domains where the model initially struggled in reasoning mode, such as multi-turn conversations, multilinguality, and everyday conversations.

Industry observers note that our final data mixture was the result of extensive ablations examining the optimal ratio of reasoning to non-reasoning tokens and the composition within each mode. The resulting SFT dataset contains 1.8B tokens: 1B in non-reasoning mode and 0.8B in reasoning mode, comprising 12 non-reasoning datasets and 10 datasets with reasoning traces. We trained for 4 epochs (~8B tokens) using BFD (best-fit decreasing) packing with the loss masked on user turns and the results from tool calls.

We will release this data mixture along with our full training scripts to enable the community to reproduce and build upon our work.

Industry observers note that after the SFT step, we performed a round of model alignment using a combination of the Tulu3 preference dataset for non-reasoning mode and upcoming synthetic preference pairs for reasoning mode, that we generated from Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-0.6B. To ensure full coverage of all domains in the non-thinking dataset, we generated complementing thinking mode preference pairs. We selected generations from Qwen3-32B as “chosen” and responses from Qwen3-0.6B as “rejected” for alignment with Anchored Preference Optimization.

Anchored Preference Optimization (APO) is a variant of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that provides a more stable optimization objective. In DPO, the reward function r_θ(x,y) measures the log-ratio of the probability of the sequence during training compared to the model at the start of training, the reference model:.

Here β controls how much the model being optimized can change relative to the reference model. The DPO loss optimizes triplets of prompts x, chosen y_w and rejected y_l responses:.

The APO objective has been shown to be more stable, and we also observed higher downstream performance in our internal ablations.

While downstream evaluations showed improvements across mathematics, science, instruction following, coding, chat, and multilingual tasks, we observed performance degradation on long context benchmarks like RULER. We traced this degradation back to the reasoning mid-training stage, where the focus on reasoning capabilities impacted long context performance. Additionally, the APO training data was limited to 24k tokens since the vast majority of our reasoning dataset fell below this length.

To mitigate this performance drop, we explored model merging as a solution.

Industry observers note that model merging is a popular and powerful technique that allows combining the strengths of different models without the computational overhead of ensembling or the need for additional training. We used the MergeKit library to perform the model merging, as it includes several merging methods, including linear and non-linear merging.

Our merging recipe consists of two steps:.

According to recent reports, the resulting model is the checkpoint we are releasing today. It maintains performance across a wide range of tasks. So let’s turn to the evaluation result both of this model as well as the base model.

Industry observers note that we evaluate base models and the instruct model both in reasoning and non-reasoning mode. Let’s first cover the base model’s performance!

The plot below indicates SmolLM3's win rate across 12 popular benchmarks evaluating knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding capabilities. SmolLM3 consistently outperforms other 3B models and achieves competitive performance with larger 4B models including Qwen3-4B and Gemma3-4B.

Evaluation benchmarks used for the win rate: HellaSwag, ARC, Winogrande, CommonsenseQA, MMLU-CF, MMLU Pro CF, PIQA, OpenBookQA, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval+, MBPP+.

Recent findings suggest that smolLM3 achieves first or second place on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks (HellaSwag, ARC, BoolQ), demonstrating strong performance in these core capabilities. Math and coding performance is competitive within the 3B class. Long-context performance on Ruler 64k reveals the model can handle extended sequences effectively.

According to recent reports, the model demonstrates strong multilingual performance across five major European languages when evaluated on multilingual benchmarks including Global MMLU, MLMM HellaSwag, Flores-200, Belebele, testing knowledge, commonsense reasoning, text understanding, and translation. This reveals SmolLM3 maintains consistent performance beyond English.

In summary, the base model highlights very strong performance across many domains. Let’s see how this translates to the instruct model’s performance.

Since SmolLM3 has both an instruct and reasoning mode we need to evaluate the model in both modes and compare to models with same capabilities.

Sources indicate that we evaluate SmolLM3 against other 3B non-reasoning models and compare it to Qwen3 reasoning models in no thinking mode across multiple benchmarks. As shown in the performance chart, SmolLM3 outperforms other 3B non-reasoning models including Llama3.2 3B Instruct and Qwen2.5 3B Instruct and sits at an efficiency sweet spot between reasoning models, significantly outperforming Qwen3 1.7B while getting close to the 4B model performance at a lower computational cost.

According to recent reports, so the instruct model sits right at the pareto front of performance and cost. Let’s see how the reasoning model does!

Sources indicate that when evaluating SmolLM3's reasoning capabilities with extended thinking enabled, the model indicates substantial improvements across most benchmarks compared to its non-reasoning counterpart. We observe notable gains in challenging tasks like AIME 2025 (36.7% vs 9.3%), competitive programming on LiveCodeBench (30.0% vs 15.2%), and graduate-level reasoning on GPQA Diamond (41.7% vs 35.7%).

Recent findings suggest that while Qwen3 4B generally achieves the highest scores across both thinking and non-thinking modes, SmolLM3 demonstrates competitive performance within the 3B parameter class, particularly excelling in mathematical reasoning and complex problem-solving tasks. The model's dual-mode capability allows users to choose between faster inference without reasoning or more thorough analysis with extended thinking.

So the last question is: how can you use the model?

The modeling code for SmolLM3 is available in transformers v4.53.0, so make sure to upgrade your transformers version. You can also load the model with the latest vllm which uses transformers as a backend.

We recommend setting temperature=0.6 and top_p=0.95 in the sampling parameters.

We enable extended thinking by default, so the example above generates the output with a reasoning trace. For choosing between enabling, you can provide the /think and /no_think flags through the system prompt as shown in the snippet below for extended thinking disabled. The code for generating the response with extended thinking would be the same except that the system prompt should have /think instead of /no_think.

Industry observers note that smolLM3 supports tool calling! Just pass your list of tools under the argument xml_tools (for standard tool-calling), or python_tools (for calling tools like python functions in a  snippet).

What is Model Routing in AI?
